sheet-1.description: The lower half of the first sheet of the April 1897 Sanborn-Perris atlas of Deckertown (today the borough of Sussex), below the heavy line that divides it from the index of specials, the small-scale key map of the four sheets and the title cartouche. Drawn at 50 feet to an inch, it covers the thinly built residential north end of the village between Bank Street on the west and Unionville Avenue on the east, from the sheet's upper border south to Spring Street and Church Street, where sheet 2 continues. Bank Street and Main Street run side by side down the left third of the sheet, separated by a long narrow block whose north end is drawn just below the dividing line; Main is drawn about 30 feet wide and Bank about 50, each with a six-inch water pipe and hydrants. Frame dwellings with stables and outbuildings stand along both streets, with a wheelwright shop near Main. In the middle of the sheet is block 1, almost empty except for a few dwellings and sheds. On the east side Unionville Avenue, also with a water pipe, runs north-north-east past scattered dwellings, and Church Street curves west from it toward Main at the bottom of the sheet; the Presbyterian Church, with its steeple and 20 feet to the eaves, stands on the north side of Church Street. A shoe factory is drawn at the corner of Main and Spring Streets. A compass rose sits in the open middle of the block. Block numbers 1, 3, 5 and 8 and the adjoining sheet number 2 are printed on the sheet.
notes: Main Street north of Newton Avenue appears to have been realigned or widened: junctions on it sat 4 to 5 m from the modern lines on sheets 1 and 2, and modern Main bends to meet Bank Street further south than the drawn streets would.
The modern Church Street / Unionville Avenue junction lies about 20 to 30 m from where both sheets 1 and 2 draw it; Unionville Avenue north of Church has probably been realigned.

Placement rests on one detected-quality junction (Bank / Spring), points carried from sheet 2 along Spring and Church Streets, and a point derived along Bank Street at the atlas scale; low confidence toward the top of the part.

map, 50 ft. Top half: index of specials, key map of the four sheets (small scale, not georeferenced) and title cartouche; below the heavy line, residential Bank, Main and Unionville Av north of Spring St, Church St and the Presbyterian Church. One part configured (the area below the heavy line). Almost no street junctions on it: placed from Bank/Spring, points carried from sheet 2 along Spring and Church Streets, and a derived point on the Bank St centreline.

sheet-2.description: Sheet 2 of the April 1897 Sanborn-Perris atlas of Deckertown, drawn at 50 feet to an inch, shows the business centre of the village (today the borough of Sussex). Main Street runs down the middle of the sheet from Spring Street to its bend into Hamburgh Avenue, lined with brick and frame stores: hardware, harness, groceries, dry goods, drugs, jewellers, clothing, a bank, the post office, lodge rooms, a bakery, a printing office and the Union Hotel and its horse sheds. Bank Street and Mill Street (today Loomis Avenue) run parallel to the west, with the M.E. Church, a livery, marble works and smaller shops; Mill Street curves round the south end of the block to rejoin Main. Newton Avenue crosses the sheet east-west and continues west over Clove Creek by a bridge; on the creek stand the Deckertown Foundry and Machine Shop on the supply race, the Horton and Lewis Cream Co. creamery, the Electric Light Station and the Wantage Bottling Works. East of Main, Church Street and Unionville Avenue lead north past the De Camp Hotel, with De Camp Place lettered in the open ground south of it. The east half of the sheet is the slope of High Hill, outlined by its foot of slope, with the Public School on it; below it Harrison Avenue, East Main and Liberty Street lay out a residential block of frame dwellings. Water pipes with hydrant numbers are drawn along the streets. The bottom margin is marked no exposure.
notes: Mill Street is today the north part of Loomis Avenue; Harrison Avenue is Harrison Street; Main (Hamburgh Avenue) south of the bend is Hamburg Avenue.
Main Street / Spring Street was left out of the fit: on both sheets 1 and 2 the drawn junction lies 4 to 5 m from the modern one; Main Street north of Newton Avenue appears realigned or widened.
Main / Newton / Unionville and Harrison / Main were hand-picked; the detector found six junctions.

map, 50 ft. Downtown: Main St from Spring St to Hamburgh Av, Bank, Mill (now Loomis Av), Newton Av, Church St, Unionville Av, Harrison Av (now Harrison St), Liberty, E. Main; Clove Creek with the creamery and electric light station. One part.

sheet-3.description: Sheet 3 of the April 1897 Sanborn-Perris atlas of Deckertown (today Sussex), at 50 feet to an inch, covers the east side of the village around the New York, Susquehanna and Western Railroad. The sheet is turned about 44 degrees from sheet 2, so that East Main and Munson Streets run up the page and Main (Hamburgh Avenue) runs across its foot. The railroad enters at the top and curves south-east across the middle; beside it stand the railroad station, the freight house and platform, coal pockets and lumber sheds of the C.A. Wilson lumber and coal yard, the Deckertown steam mill, grist and saw mills on Cross Street, and the Decker and Simmons lumber yard with its sheds and feed store near the bottom. West of the tracks, the blocks between East Main, Liberty and Munson Streets hold dwellings, a general store and the Baptist Church; the Harrison House and the Wantage House stand east of Munson, along an unnamed street marked St. No Name. North-east of the railroad, Walnut Street, Second Street and Sycamore Street lay out residential blocks with a private school; Chestnut Street is noted as beyond the top of the sheet. Along Main (Hamburgh Avenue) at the bottom are dwellings, a blacksmith, tin and paint shops, an ice house and the Deckertown laundry. Water pipes with hydrant numbers run along most streets.
notes: Second is today 2nd Street; Main (Hamburgh Avenue) is Hamburg Avenue; the street marked St. No Name is today New Street.

The N.Y.S. and W. railroad through Deckertown is abandoned; part of its line is today 1st Street, and modern Munson Street runs north from Liberty Street to Walnut Street along the old station approach, which the sheet does not draw as a street.
Second Street / Sycamore Street was left out: the modern street bends east before meeting Sycamore, away from the drawn corner.

map, 50 ft. E. Main, Munson, Cross, Liberty, Walnut, Second, Sycamore and Main (Hamburgh Av, now Hamburg Avenue); N.Y.S.&W. R.R. station, freight house and lumber yards. Turned about 44 degrees from sheet 2. One part.

sheet-4-1.description: The main, lower part of sheet 4 of the April 1897 Deckertown atlas shows Hamburgh, a separate village four and a half miles south of Deckertown (today the borough of Hamburg), drawn at 50 feet to an inch with north to the left of the page. North Avenue, the Deckertown Road, crosses the part from left to right and continues as Church; Wallkill Avenue (the Newton road) leaves it on the left, Vernon Avenue (the McAfee road) on the right, and Orchard Avenue leads from it past Main to Orchard Street along the foot of the part. The Hamburgh Hotel with its stables, the Episcopal Church and rectory face North Avenue; the National Hotel stands on Orchard Street, and Thomas Fountain's broom factory lies west of Wallkill Avenue. At the corner of Orchard Avenue and Main are a general store, hardware and stoves, a tin shop and the post office, and along Main further stores, a drug store, a saloon, a grocer, a barber, shoemaker and dwellings; the Baptist Church and the public school stand on Church. A note in the lower right gives Hamburgh's population as 400, with no steam or hand engine, no hose carts, poor water facilities and prevailing north-west winds. The rest of the part is open lots and scattered frame dwellings; the strip above the heavy line holds the Deckertown blocks of part 2 and the Hamburgh railroad strip of part 3.
notes: North Avenue (Deckertown Road) and Church are today Hamburg Turnpike; Orchard Avenue lies on the line of modern Ames Boulevard, and Orchard Street is Orchard Street.
Vernon Avenue and Main have been realigned at their junctions with the modern Ames Boulevard; neither junction was used.

The fit puts the part at about 9.0 px per foot against about 8.0 on the Deckertown sheets: the Hamburgh part appears drawn about 10 percent larger than the stated 50 feet to an inch, or the modern junctions have moved; four points only.

sheet-4-2.description: The upper left part of sheet 4 of the April 1897 Deckertown atlas, drawn at 50 feet to an inch and continuing the east side of sheet 3, shows the residential blocks between Walnut Street and Sycamore Street in Deckertown (today Sussex). Third Street and Fourth Street run up the part, each with a water pipe and hydrants, and Thompson Street runs parallel further east, its east edge drawn as a broken line. The blocks hold a handful of frame dwellings and outbuildings, a private school at the corner of Walnut and the edge of the part, and much open ground; block 32, between Fourth and Thompson, is mostly empty and carries the place name Deckertown. A row of lots on the south side of Sycamore Street is cut by the heavy line that separates this part from the Hamburgh map below. An arrow in block 31 points toward the railroad, and lot numbers run along the street fronts.
notes: Third and Fourth are today 3rd Street and 4th Street; Thompson appears to be today's Grove Street, though its modern junction with Walnut Street lies about 12 m from the drawn one and was not used.
Placed from four detected junctions only (3rd and 4th Streets with Walnut and Sycamore).
